The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Use natural units $\hbar=c=1$ on Minkowski spacetime $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dt\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and spatial orientation $\epsilon_{123}=1$. Fix the global gauge group $SU(2)$, not $SO(3)$, and the trivial right principal $SU(2)$-bundle over each spatial slice. Let

$$T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a\quad(a=1,2,3),\qquad \kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY),$$

where $\sigma_a$ are the Pauli matrices and $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has basis $T_1,T_2,T_3$. Thus $[T_a,T_b]=\epsilon_{abc}T_c$ and $\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$. The positive coupling $g$ is dimensionless. The scalar field is one real adjoint Higgs field: a smooth $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued map $\Phi$ on $\mathbb R^3$, viewed as the real form in the complexified adjoint representation. A gauge connection is a smooth $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued one-form $A=A_i dx^i$. In a local section change $s_j=s_i h_{ij}$, use the right-action convention $A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{h_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+h_{ij}^{-1}dh_{ij}$ and $\Phi_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{h_{ij}^{-1}}\Phi_i$. Define

$$F_{ij}=\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i+[A_i,A_j],\qquad D_i\Phi=\partial_i\Phi+[A_i,\Phi],\qquad B_i=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}.$$

The static Prasad–Sommerfield sector has $\partial_tA_i=\partial_t\Phi=0$, $A_0=0$, no other dynamical fields, and identically zero Higgs potential. Its adopted energy functional is

$$E[A,\Phi]=\frac{1}{2g^2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{i=1}^3\bigl(\kappa(B_i,B_i)+\kappa(D_i\Phi,D_i\Phi)\bigr)\,d^3x.$$

The field dimensions are $[A_i]=[\Phi]=\mathrm{length}^{-1}$ and $[F_{ij}]=[B_i]=[D_i\Phi]=\mathrm{length}^{-2}$, so $E$ has dimension $\mathrm{length}^{-1}$. A configuration is finite-energy when this integral is finite.

The boundary data fix a number $v>0$ of dimension $\mathrm{length}^{-1}$ and require $|\Phi|_\kappa\to v$ and $n_\infty(\omega):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\Phi(R\omega)/v$ to exist smoothly on the unit sphere $S^2$ of spatial directions. Here $|X|_\kappa^2:=\kappa(X,X)$. The limiting tangential covariant derivative of $n_\infty$ vanishes, and the limiting magnetic field lies in the pointwise stabilizer Lie algebra $\{X\in\mathfrak{su}(2):[X,n_\infty(\omega)]=0\}$. The stabilizer subgroup of $T_3$ is $U(1)=\{\exp(\theta T_3):\theta\in\mathbb R/(4\pi\mathbb Z)\}$. On closed northern and southern hemispheres choose smooth local lifts $u_N,u_S$ with $\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha}T_3=n_\infty$; their equatorial transition is $u_S=u_N h$ with $h(\varphi)=\exp(\theta(\varphi)T_3)$, where $\varphi\in[0,2\pi]$ parametrizes the equator and $\theta:[0,2\pi]\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth lift. The local adapted frames, connection forms, and curvature forms extend smoothly, respectively $C^1$, to open neighborhoods of the closed hemispheres. The surface limit below exists. The admissible external Wilson probes include the fundamental doublet, on which $T_3$ has weights $\pm\tfrac12$; this specifies the electric probe lattice without adding a propagating fundamental matter field. Define the classical magnetic surface charge and its energy normalization by

$$m:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R^2}\kappa(\Phi,B_i)\,\hat x_i\,dS,\qquad T:=g^{-2}m,$$

where $\hat x=x/|x|$ is the outward unit normal and $dS$ is Euclidean area. The transition increment $\theta(2\pi)-\theta(0)$ is not assumed to be quantized in this definition. These are adopted classical model data; they assert no empirical law, quantum continuum construction, supersymmetry representation, or quantum BPS state.

Assume the axiom of countable choice. Let
$G=SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\}$ with its real Lie-group
structure. Define the Pauli matrices
$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and put
$T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ for $a\in\{1,2,3\}$. Then $G$ is compact and
noncommutative, its real Lie algebra has basis $T_1,T_2,T_3$ with
$[T_a,T_b]=\sum_{c=1}^3\epsilon_{abc}T_c$, and the real bilinear form
$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is positive
definite, symmetric, and invariant under
$\operatorname{Ad}_gX=gXg^{-1}$, with $\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

derivations.claim: In either limiting adapted frame, $n_\infty=T_3$ and $D_{\mathrm{tan}}n_\infty=0$, so $[\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty},T_3]=0$. Writing $\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}=a_\alpha^1T_1+a_\alpha^2T_2+a_\alpha^3T_3$, the commutator relations in [F2] give $[\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty},T_3]=a_\alpha^2T_1-a_\alpha^1T_2$; hence $\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}=a_\alpha T_3$ for a real $C^1$ one-form $a_\alpha$. Its curvature is $\mathcal F_{\alpha,\infty}=da_\alpha\,T_3$, since $[T_3,T_3]=0$.

For finite $R$, the two-form $F$ pulled back by $\iota_R$ is the magnetic flux form: $\iota_R^*F=(B_i\hat x_i)\,dS_R$ under the outward orientation. By $\operatorname{Ad}$-invariance of $\kappa$ and the frame definitions, the flux at radius $R$ therefore satisfies  $$\frac{1}{v}\int_{S_R^2}\kappa(\Phi,B_i)\hat x_i\,dS=\sum_{\alpha=N,S}\int_{D_\alpha}\kappa(q_{\alpha,R},\mathcal F_{\alpha,R}).$$  The uniform limits of $q_{\alpha,R}$ and $\mathcal F_{\alpha,R}$ imply uniform convergence of the integrands to $\kappa(T_3,\mathcal F_{\alpha,\infty})$. Each hemisphere has finite area, so the absolute difference of its integrals is bounded by its area times the sup norm of the integrand difference and tends to zero. Using $\kappa(T_3,T_3)=1$, we obtain $m/v=\sum_\alpha\int_{D_\alpha}\kappa(T_3,\mathcal F_{\alpha,\infty})=\int_{D_N}da_N+\int_{D_S}da_S$.

Apply [F3] separately to the two closed hemispheres. Their induced equatorial orientations are opposite, so $\int_{D_N}da_N+\int_{D_S}da_S=\int_C(a_N-a_S)$. The limiting right-action transition stated above, with $h=\exp(\theta T_3)$, and the fact that both limiting forms lie in the stabilizer algebra give $a_S=a_N+d\theta$. Therefore the flux is $-\int_Cd\theta=-(\theta(2\pi)-\theta(0))$.

In the fundamental representation, $\exp(	heta T_3)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i	heta/2},e^{i	heta/2})$. Since $h$ is a closed SU(2) loop, equality of its endpoint matrices gives $e^{-i(	heta(2\pi)-	heta(0))/2}=1$, hence $	heta(2\pi)-	heta(0)=4\pi k$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. The definition $
u=-k$ and step 3.1 yield $m/v=4\pi
u$, so $m=4\pi v
u$ and $T=4\pi v
u/g^2$.

For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

derivations.claim: Define $J_i=\kappa(\Phi,B_i)$. The product rule gives $\partial_iJ_i=\kappa(\partial_i\Phi,B_i)+\kappa(\Phi,\partial_iB_i)$. By [F1]–[F3], the sum is $\kappa(D_i\Phi,B_i)+\kappa(\Phi,D_iB_i)=\kappa(D_i\Phi,B_i)$: the two connection terms cancel by Ad-invariance and $D_iB_i=0$ by Bianchi.

On each closed ball $B_R$, $J$ is $C^1$, so [F4] and step 1.1 give $\int_{B_R}\sum_i\kappa(D_i\Phi,B_i)\,d^3x=\int_{S_R^2}\kappa(\Phi,B_i)\hat x_i\,dS$. Positive definiteness in [F2] gives $2|\kappa(D_i\Phi,B_i)|\le\kappa(D_i\Phi,D_i\Phi)+\kappa(B_i,B_i)$, so finite energy makes the cross term integrable. Taking $R\to\infty$ and using the declared surface limit yields $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_i\kappa(B_i,D_i\Phi)\,d^3x=m$.

Expand the first square: its integral is $\int\sum_i\bigl(\kappa(B_i,B_i)+\kappa(D_i\Phi,D_i\Phi)-2\kappa(B_i,D_i\Phi)\bigr)\,d^3x$. By [F1] the first two terms give $2g^2E$, and by step 2.1 the cross term integrates to $2m$; multiplying by $1/(2g^2)$ and adding $T=m/g^2$ gives the first identity. Expanding with the plus sign changes the cross term to $+2m$, so subtracting $T$ gives the second identity. All integrals converge by [F1], [F2], and step 2.1.

Each square integral in step 3.1 is nonnegative by [F2], giving $E\ge T$ and $E\ge -T$, hence $E\ge|T|$. For $T>0$, equality in $E\ge T$ holds exactly when the integral of the continuous nonnegative function $\sum_i\kappa(B_i-D_i\Phi,B_i-D_i\Phi)$ is zero, which is equivalent to $B_i=D_i\Phi$ everywhere; the converse follows from the first identity. For $T<0$, the second identity gives equivalently $B_i=-D_i\Phi$. For $T=0$, equality means $E=0$; positivity and continuity of the energy density imply $B_i=D_i\Phi=0$ everywhere, and these conditions also make $E=0$.

On oriented Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ with $\epsilon_{123}=1$, use the zero-potential static model with global group $SU(2)$, $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2$, $\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$, $F_{ij}=\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i+[A_i,A_j]$, $D_i\Phi=\partial_i\Phi+[A_i,\Phi]$, and $B_i=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$. Let $g>0$ be dimensionless, $v>0$ of dimension $\mathrm{length}^{-1}$, and $A_i,\Phi$ be smooth static fields. Assume $|\Phi|_\kappa\to v$, $\Phi(R\omega)/v\to n_\infty(\omega)$ smoothly, $D_{\mathrm{tan}}n_\infty=0$, and $B_\infty$ takes values in the centralizer of $n_\infty$. Let $D_N,D_S\subset S^2$ be the closed northern and southern hemispheres, and choose smooth lifts $u_\alpha$ on neighborhoods of $D_\alpha$ with $\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha}T_3=n_\infty$ and transition $u_S=u_Nh$ on their common equator, where $h(\varphi)=\exp(\theta(\varphi)T_3)$ and $\theta:[0,2\pi]\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth lift. For $\iota_R:S^2\to S_R^2$, $\iota_R(\omega)=R\omega$, define on each $D_\alpha$ the fixed-frame angular connection, curvature, and normalized Higgs field by

$$\mathcal A_{\alpha,R}:=\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}(\iota_R^*A)+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha,\qquad \mathcal F_{\alpha,R}:=\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}(\iota_R^*F),\qquad q_{\alpha,R}:=\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}\bigl(\Phi(R\,\cdot)/v\bigr).$$

Assume that $\mathcal A_{\alpha,R}$ converges pointwise on each closed hemisphere to $\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}$, which extends as a $C^1$ one-form to a neighborhood of $D_\alpha$. Define its curvature by $\mathcal F_{\alpha,\infty}:=d\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}+\tfrac12[\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}\wedge\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}]$, and assume it extends as a $C^1$ two-form to a neighborhood of $D_\alpha$. Also assume $\mathcal F_{\alpha,R}\to\mathcal F_{\alpha,\infty}$ uniformly on each closed hemisphere. The fixed-frame right-action transition gives $\mathcal A_{S,\infty}=\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}\mathcal A_{N,\infty}+h^{-1}dh$. The smooth Higgs-field limit gives $q_{\alpha,R}\to T_3$ uniformly. The condition $D_{\mathrm{tan}}n_\infty=0$ uses the limiting adapted connections $\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}$. The equator is oriented as the boundary of $D_N$, and the admissible external electric probes include the fundamental doublet. If the surface flux limit

$$m=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R^2}\kappa(\Phi,B_i)\hat x_i\,dS$$

exists, define

$$\nu:=-\frac{\theta(2\pi)-\theta(0)}{4\pi}.$$

Then $\nu\in\mathbb Z$ and the classical magnetic surface charge and energy-normalized surface term are

$$m=4\pi v\nu,\qquad T=\frac{m}{g^2}=\frac{4\pi v}{g^2}\nu.$$

This is flux quantization for the stated global form, boundary reduction, and probe lattice; it does not assert a universal normalization for other groups or global forms.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Use natural units on Minkowski $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and oriented Euclidean spatial slice with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. Fix the global group $SU(2)$, basis $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2$, and positive $\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant form $\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$ with $\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$. Let $g>0$ be dimensionless and let $A_i,\Phi$ be smooth static fields in the zero-potential adjoint-Higgs model, with $[A_i]=[\Phi]=\mathrm{length}^{-1}$, $F_{ij}=\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i+[A_i,A_j]$, $D_i\Phi=\partial_i\Phi+[A_i,\Phi]$, and $B_i=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$. Require the model's smooth finite-energy boundary reduction: $|\Phi|_\kappa\to v>0$ for a fixed $v$ of dimension $\mathrm{length}^{-1}$, with smooth $n_\infty=\Phi/v$, the limiting tangential covariant derivative of $n_\infty$ vanishes, and the limiting magnetic field lies in its stabilizer algebra. Suppose the energy

$$E=\frac{1}{2g^2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_i\bigl(\kappa(B_i,B_i)+\kappa(D_i\Phi,D_i\Phi)\bigr)\,d^3x$$

is finite and the model's asymptotic reduction and surface limit

$$m=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R^2}\kappa(\Phi,B_i)\hat x_i\,dS$$

exist. Put $T=m/g^2$. Then both identities hold:

$$E=\frac{1}{2g^2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_i\kappa(B_i-D_i\Phi,B_i-D_i\Phi)\,d^3x+T,$$

$$E=\frac{1}{2g^2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_i\kappa(B_i+D_i\Phi,B_i+D_i\Phi)\,d^3x-T.$$

Consequently $E\ge |T|$. If $T>0$, equality holds exactly when $B_i=D_i\Phi$ for every $i$ and every $x$; if $T<0$, equality holds exactly when $B_i=-D_i\Phi$ everywhere. If $T=0$, equality holds exactly when $B_i=0$ and $D_i\Phi=0$ everywhere. These are conditional classical deductions for the adopted energy functional; the word BPS here refers only to classical energy saturation and asserts no quantum state or supersymmetry central-charge relation.

derivations.claim: The Taylor expansions $\sinh u=u+u^3/6+O(u^5)$ and $\cosh u=1+u^2/2+O(u^4)$ give $H(u)=u/3+O(u^3)$ and $K(u)=1-u^2/6+O(u^4)$. Hence $H(u)/u$ and $(1-K(u))/u^2$ are analytic in $u^2$ near zero; writing $n_a=x_a/r$ shows $\Phi^a=-v^2x_a/3+O(r^2x_a)$ and $A_i^a=(v^2/6+O(r^2))\epsilon_{aij}x_j$. Thus both fields extend smoothly through the origin.
For $u>0$, differentiation gives $H'(u)=1/u^2-1/\sinh^2u=(1-K(u)^2)/u^2$ and $K'(u)=K(u)(1/u-\coth u)=-K(u)H(u)$. Also $\partial_i n_a=(\delta_{ia}-n_in_a)/r$.

Substitution into $D_i\Phi=\partial_i\Phi+[A_i,\Phi]$ gives the ordinary derivative $-v^2H'(u)n_in_a-vH(u)(\delta_{ia}-n_in_a)/r$. The commutator term is $vH(u)(1-K(u))(\delta_{ia}-n_in_a)/r$, using $\epsilon_{abc}\epsilon_{bij}n_jn_c=n_in_a-\delta_{ia}$. Thus $D_i\Phi^a=-v^2H'(u)n_in_a-vH(u)K(u)(\delta_{ia}-n_in_a)/r=-(1-K(u)^2)n_in_a/r^2+vK'(u)(\delta_{ia}-n_in_a)/r$, by step 1.2 and $u=vr$.

Write $A_i^a=f(r)\epsilon_{aij}x_j$ with $f(r)=(1-K(vr))/r^2$. Direct differentiation gives $\partial_iA_j^a-\partial_jA_i^a=f'(r)r(n_i\epsilon_{aj\ell}n_\ell-n_j\epsilon_{ai\ell}n_\ell)-2f(r)\epsilon_{aij}$. The commutator is $[A_i,A_j]^a=f(r)^2r^2\epsilon_{ij\ell}n_\ell n_a$, since $(e_i\times n)\times(e_j\times n)=\epsilon_{ij\ell}n_\ell n$. Contracting their sum with $\epsilon_{kij}/2$ and substituting $f=(1-K(vr))/r^2$ yields $B_k^a=-(1-K(u)^2)n_kn_a/r^2+vK'(u)(\delta_{ka}-n_kn_a)/r$. This equals step 2.1, so $B_i=D_i\Phi$ for $r>0$, and smoothness extends the equality to $r=0$.

As $u\to\infty$, $H(u)=1-u^{-1}+O(e^{-2u})$, $H'(u)=O(u^{-2})$, and $K(u),K'(u)=O(ue^{-u})$. The formulas in steps 2.1 and 3.1 therefore give $B_i,D_i\Phi=O(r^{-2})$ at infinity, whose squared magnitude is integrable because $\int_1^\infty r^2r^{-4}\,dr<\infty$; smoothness gives local integrability at the origin. Thus the energy is finite. The radial component is $B_i^a n_i=-(1-K(u)^2)n_a/r^2$, while $\Phi^a=-vH(u)n_a$, so $\kappa(\Phi,B_i)n_i=vH(u)(1-K(u)^2)/r^2$. Taking the surface limit gives $m=4\pi v$.

Let $\omega\in S^2$, so $n_\infty(\omega)=-\omega_aT_a$, and choose smooth lifts $u_N,u_S$ on neighborhoods of the closed hemispheres with $\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha}T_3=n_\infty$. With $\iota_R(\omega)=R\omega$, the given gauge potential has angular pullback $\iota_R^*A=-(1-K(vR))(\omega\times d\omega)_aT_a$. Since $K(vR)\to0$ and is independent of $\omega$, the adapted connections $\mathcal A_{\alpha,R}=\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}(\iota_R^*A)+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$ converge in $C^1$ on each closed hemisphere to the $C^1$ form $\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}= -\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}((\omega\times d\omega)_aT_a)+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$. The radial magnetic field from step 3.1 gives $\mathcal F_{\alpha,R}=\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}(\iota_R^*F)=(1-K(vR)^2)T_3\,d\Omega$, where $d\Omega$ is the outward area form of the unit sphere; hence these angular curvature forms converge uniformly to $T_3\,d\Omega$, the curvature of $\mathcal A_{\alpha,\infty}$. In the same fixed frames, $q_{\alpha,R}=\operatorname{Ad}_{u_\alpha^{-1}}(\Phi(R\omega)/v)=H(vR)T_3\to T_3$ uniformly. Thus the profile satisfies the flux theorem's fixed-frame curvature-limit and Higgs-limit hypotheses.

By [F3] and step 4.1, $4\pi v=m=4\pi v\nu$, so $\nu=1$ because $v>0$. Then $T=4\pi v/g^2>0$. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $B_i=D_i\Phi$, so [F4] gives $E=T=4\pi v/g^2$. This verifies a classical unit-flux first-order solution and its saturation without asserting a quantum state.
